paragraphs: Rav Yosef (in the Yerushalmi: Yosi), son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. In [Bava Batra 10b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.10b.5) (supplied: בב״ב י:) it is related that he once fell ill and 'was in a trance' (he grew weak and they thought he had died, and afterward he rose from his illness). His father said to him: What did you see? He said to him: I saw an upside-down world: the upper ones below and the lower ones above. He said to him: You saw a clear world, etc. And in כו״ר (abbreviation retained as supplied), at the beginning of [section] 3 (supplied: רפ״ג), Hyman considers the incident mistakenly cited in the name of R' Meisha, son of the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

(And in [Tosafot](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosafot_on_Bava_Batra.10b.5.1), s.v. 'Elyonim' [the upper ones], פ״ח (retained as supplied; the named Vilna Tosafot parallel reads פי׳ ר״ח): that they had a tradition that the upside-down world he saw was that Shmuel was sitting before Rav Yehuda his student, end quote. Hyman argues: And there is no proof from this that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lived until after the death of Rav Yehuda, for that is an impossibility; but without doubt ר״ת (abbreviation retained as supplied) had the reading as in Yuchasin, that Rabbi Yosef son of R' Yehoshua fell ill.) Hyman further says that Rav Yosef received [teachings] from his father, as we find in [Chullin 56b](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.56b.4).

There he inquired of his father. And in Taanit ch. 1 halakhah 4 ([compare Yerushalmi Taanit 1:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.1.6.5)): Ze'ira bar Chama, Yosi son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. And in Yoma ch. 5 halakhah 1 ([compare Yerushalmi Yoma 8:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yoma.8.1.5)) Hyman reports an error there. Hyman relates that the house of the Nasi took him as a son-in-law, as in [Kiddushin 33b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.33b.7-8), where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: I am not worthy to stand before my son, but only out of respect for the house of the Nasi. Hyman concludes that he lived long after his father, as in [Yoma 78a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.78a.9),

where Ze'ira bar Chama, the host of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said to Rav Yosef, the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: “Son of a lion!” [בר אריה] Come and I will tell you an excellent thing that your father used to say. Hyman therefore argues that what is cited in קה״ר (abbreviation retained as supplied) at פ״י־ה (locator kept as supplied; possibly 10:5, unresolved), that his son swallowed a snake and died in his father's lifetime, refers to another son whom Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had, as Hyman says, “we have explained at length,” in the entry R' Meisha, son of the son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.[^9]

The whole saved Vilna Tosafot on Bava Batra 10b, Elyonim comment, reads פי׳ ר״ח and attributes the received tradition about Shmuel sitting before Rav Yehuda to the Geonim. It is a positive digital comparison for the supplied פ״ח, which remains visible; it does not establish the printed letters or expand Hyman’s separate ר״ת. The whole Davidson Yoma 78a paragraph explicitly names Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rav Yosef his son, addressing the latter as “Son of a lion”; these support the local full titles and vocative, without adding a Bar Aryeh patronymic. Hyman’s father-used-to-SAY wording remains distinct from the paragraph’s used-to-DO. The whole Torat Emet Kohelet Rabbah 10:5 paragraph has חד בלעא and a healing/verse episode without explicitly writing נחש; Hyman’s snake wording, other-son identification and chronological conclusion remain his reports. His rejection as impossible and “without doubt” reconstruction retain their force. The separate Yuchasin, כו״ר, Jerusalem Talmud, Chullin and Kiddushin passages were not freshly collated here. The uncollated Meisha and shortened Yehoshua pointers use R'; fully written רבי in the Yuchasin report remains Rabbi. No identity, genealogy, teacher or chronology fact is admitted, and all three source holds and existing mixed notes remain intact.

Bava Batra 10b names Yosef son of Rabbi Yehoshua in the inverted-world story. The consulted Pesachim 50a parallel names Rav Yosef son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. The Vilna Tosafot comment cites a Geonic tradition under פי׳ ר״ח. In the printed Hyman II, p. 752, the abbreviation there appears as פ״רח, and the later attribution appears to read לר״ח. The supplied פ״ח and לר״ת remain in the translation. Hyman’s separate Yuchasin comparison and his contention that the alternative chronology is impossible and his reconstruction beyond doubt remain his claims. Ruth Rabbah 3:1 is a close comparison for Hyman’s opening midrash reference. The consulted version names Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua, who recovered after three days and told his father of a world in which people honored here were disgraced there. Hyman calls the attribution mistaken. The version itself does not decide that judgment or establish the exact letters of his supplied siglum.

Hyman II, p. 752, prints Taanit 1:6 and Yoma 8:1, where the consulted Yerushalmi passages preserve different transmission chains for the washing ruling. Taanit names Yosi son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Yoma has Zeura bar Chama and the accompanying bracketed name Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Hanina. The supplied chapter and halakhah numbers remain in the translation. Chullin 56b directly has Rav Yosef inquire of his father. Kiddushin 33b names the father but leaves his son unnamed, and the argument about standing for a son who is his teacher continues. The named translation explains the honor of the Nasi’s household with a marriage gloss, while Hyman draws his own biographical connection.

Hyman explicitly writes ‘swallowed a snake’ in the printed Yosef notice. The consulted Kohelet Rabbah 10:5 describes a bala involving an unnamed son, while Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 14:4 and Avodah Zarah 2:2:7 say grandson and describe recovery of breath, followed by the sage’s remark about death and the narrator’s statement that it happened as an error issuing from a ruler. Guggenheimer’s notes take this to mean that the grandson died. The Hebrew of these consulted passages has no explicit snake noun. Hyman’s separate Meisha notice (III, pp. 881–882) glosses the obstruction as something that choked the sufferer and proposes that the son was Meisha’s father. Hyman’s reconstruction, including his distinction between the sons, remains attributed. Yoma 78a has Zeira address Rav Yosef as ‘Son of a lion’ and describes what his father used to do, while Hyman says ‘used to say.’ The episode itself gives no interval of years.

The inverted-world account in [Pesachim 50a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.50a.6) fully names Rav Yosef son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. [Ruth Rabbah 3:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Ruth_Rabbah.3.1) instead tells a related story about Meyasha, a grandson. [Kohelet Rabbah 10:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Kohelet_Rabbah.10.5.1) describes an unnamed son. The parallel narratives in [Yerushalmi Shabbat 14:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Shabbat.14.4.8) and [Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 2:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Avodah_Zarah.2.2.7) say grandson and do not explicitly name a snake. These accounts underlie, but do not settle, Hyman’s proposal of another son.
